title: Steve Popper: NBA champion Knicks have target on their backs
text:
Steve Popper: NBA champion Knicks have target on their backs - Newsday Skip to content Menu Today's paper Long Island Sports News Investigations Restaurants Opinion Business Things to Do Schools Obits Newsday TV Search TOGETHER LI Steve Popper Watch highlights Scores and stats Columnists Sports Columnists Steve Popper Steve Popper: NBA champion Knicks have target on their backs
 Knicks' Jalen Brunson reacts during the second quarter against the Detroit Pistons at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday. Credit: Jim McIsaac
 By Steve Popper steve.popper@newsday.com @StevePopper Updated October 27, 2026 9:43 pm Share In another time, another circumstance, the Knicks might have viewed the arrival of the Detroit Pistons at Madison Square Garden Tuesday night as the sort of early-season test to serve as a measuring stick — the opponent a team that manhandled them even in the Knicks championship season and one that arrived with a perfect record. 
 But the Knicks seemed much more focused on themselves as they readied for the game. It was the 0-3 record they brought into the night , one of just five teams in NBA history to begin a title defense with three straight losses. 
 It was the numbers. They ran dead last in points per game, 29th in field goal percentage and last in pace. And maybe most of all, it was clear to the eye test: things just haven’t looked like they did when the Knicks finished off a historic postseason run. 
 Maybe some flaws last season were hidden by the heroics of Jalen Brunson, who seemed to come up big down the stretch of so many come-from-behind wins. He has been good, but not the lifesaver, so far this season. And when the last loss was over, he simplified the task. 
 “Find whatever it takes to win,” Brunson said. “Control what we can control. Focus on the little details that might seem small but can impact winning. Most importantly, stick together. One thing I’ve said during training camp and to this day is we’re going to see who we are within the first couple weeks of the season. And we’re seeing adversity so how are we going to respond? 
 “We’re going to get everyone’s best because of last year. Everyone has been telling us what a great job we did, how fun it was, what we did for the city, the constant praise and so we need to be the opposite.” 
 The experience and maturity of the team would tell you that they will. They returned nearly the entire rotation intact, they discovered the best ways to play together along their postseason path and they certainly know how to respond to any challenge. 
 But, still, they lost those first three games and did it in a fashion that wasn’t indicating that they deserved to win those games. 
 “We have to concentrate on the next opponent in front of us, and Detroit happens to be that opponent,” Mike Brown said before Tuesday’s nationally-televised game. 
 “And, they had our number last year, you know. It is what it is, that’s kind of how the NBA is [and] it works. I said this before, one of the years we won it when I was in Golden State as an assistant. We lost the season series to Utah, I don’t know, it was 0-4, 1-3. One game, we got I think, beat by 40. 
 “So, you know, I don’t necessarily take a ton of [stock in it]. Obviously, you want to win, you want to be in good position for a playoff run, but I don’t take a ton of stock in, they won this series or they killed us in this [regular season] series because playoff season is a different ballgame.” 
 You have to squint very hard to look back at the start of last season, before the parades and trophies, when Brown took over and the Knicks were 2-3 after five games and frankly, dysfunctional. 
 Josh Hart was not only coming off the bench, but left to sit out fourth quarters as games got away and Brown was just learning about the group. 
 It may have seemed as if the Knicks were past that with the experience of last season. But, Brown said he’s still finding the way with the group this season. Bench pieces are still finding their fits and the rotation is still uncertain. 
 “No, no, no, no. You can always get better,” Brown said when asked if those issues were gone in Year 2 of his tenure. “You guys probably don’t notice, you probably never picked up on it but in Games 1 and 2 [of this season], my big experimentation was playing [Karl-Anthony Towns] and Jalen in two stretches together. And so the middle of it, I had both KAT and Jalen off the floor. We didn’t really do that last year. 
 “Watching it, I didn’t like it. So last game was the first game that I went back to [keeping one on the floor]. So there’s some things that I’m looking at or messing with that may or may not stay the same. 
 “That’s part of what you’re trying to do to figure out what’s best for your team long term. In the short term, it might not turn out good, like it didn’t turn out good not starting Josh, we took our lumps. But it was good to go through it last year. So, it’s something we’ll continue to try to figure out early on.” 
 The whole team has taken the lumps and maybe that will pay off in the long run, but it doesn’t make it any less painful right now.
 By Steve Popper steve.popper@newsday.com @StevePopper 
 Steve Popper covers the Knicks for Newsday. He has spent nearly three decades covering the Knicks and the NBA, along with just about every sports team in the New York metropolitan area.
